article_title: Typology of Generative AI Tools for Education
citation: Matt Bower, Jodie Torrington, Jennifer W. M. Lai. (2026). 2026 Typology of Generative AI Tools for Education. https://bit.ly/2026GenAITypologyData
title: Typology of Generative AI Tools for Education: nine categories of educator-used generative AI tools
description: A taxonomy arranging generative AI tools used in educational contexts into nine categories: General-Purpose Large Language Models, Image Creation Tools, Audio and Music Generation Tools, Video Generation Tools, Presentation Generation Tools, Research and Study Tools, AI Tutoring and Chatbots, Custom Education Tools, and Other Miscellaneous Tools. It continues the authors' earlier Web 2.0 and free web-based learning technology typologies, and each tool receives a brief description and link so educators can judge fit for their teaching and learning contexts.
requirements: Tools included must have been reported by two or more educators and be publicly available with a free version
constraints: Not an exhaustive list; represents a snapshot of educator-reported usage in 2025-2026
Some tools offer functionality across multiple categories
target_learners: educators across early childhood, elementary, high school and higher education
target_learning_goals: informed selection of generative AI tools aligned with pedagogical goals and values
examples: ChatGPT appears in the General-Purpose Large Language Models, Image Creation Tools, and Presentation Generation Tools categories, reflecting educators' use of this tool for multiple purposes
key_sources: Matt Bower, Jodie Torrington, Jennifer W. M. Lai. (2026). 2026 Typology of Generative AI Tools for Education. https://bit.ly/2026GenAITypologyData

citation: Salthouse, T. (2012). Consequences of Age-Related Cognitive Declines. Annual Review of Psychology, 63, 201-226. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-psych-120710-100328
title: Typical versus maximal performance distinction as an explanation for absent real-world consequences of cognitive decline
description: This explanatory account holds that everyday outcomes reflect typical functioning whereas cognitive tests assess maximal functioning, so age-related deficits appear only when demands approach maximal levels. The review states: "what we do in daily life reflects our typical level of functioning, whereas cognitive tests attempt to assess our maximal level of functioning". Because people seldom need to function at their maximum, declines may go undetected in daily-life criteria. The review presents this as the first of four candidate explanations for the lab-life discrepancy.
requirements: Outcome criteria must reflect typical rather than maximal performance for the discrepancy to arise
constraints: The account does not deny real declines; it holds they are not detected because people seldom function at the level where deficits would appear
target_learning_goals: explaining why laboratory-measured cognitive declines do not necessarily impair everyday occupational and daily functioning
examples: The review contrasts the age distribution of top-scoring reasoning performers, which peaks before age 30, with the age distribution of Fortune 500 CEOs, which peaks near 60
key_sources: Salthouse, T. (2012). Consequences of Age-Related Cognitive Declines. Annual Review of Psychology, 63, 201-226. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-psych-120710-100328

article_title: Studying Expert Practices to Create Learning Goals for Electronics Labs
citation: Benjamin Pollard, Noah Finkelstein and H. J. Lewandowski. (2014). Studying Expert Practices to Create Learning Goals for Electronics Labs. https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.3316
title: Two-dimensional framework for classifying electronics use in research labs: five Type categories and four Interaction categories
description: The article develops a framework for classifying instances of electronics use in research labs along two dimensions. The Type dimension — "referring to the type of electronics content knowledge needed for the work" — comprises Analog, Digital, Programming, Black Box, and Safety categories, with Safety "added during coding as an emergent category." The Interaction dimension — "referring to how researchers interacted with their equipment" — comprises Design, Build, Use, and Fix, with Fix also emergent. Categories are distinct but "not meant to be mutually exclusive."
requirements: Instance coding along two dimensions (Type and Interaction) based on interview responses
constraints: Categories are distinct but not mutually exclusive
Some Type-Interaction combinations are incompatible and explicitly forbidden in coding (e.g., Designing/Building a Black Box; Programming Fix, coded as Programming Design)
target_learning_goals: electronics lab skills relevant to research practice
examples: Analog example: a servo loop to lock a laser to a cavity; Fix example: isolating and replacing an op-amp in a damaged microscope
key_sources: Benjamin Pollard, Noah Finkelstein and H. J. Lewandowski. (2014). Studying Expert Practices to Create Learning Goals for Electronics Labs. https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.3316

article_title: Assessing the interactivity and prescriptiveness of faculty professional development workshops: The Real-Time Professional Development Observation Tool (R-PDOT)
citation: Alice Olmstead and Chandra Turpen. (2016). Assessing the interactivity and prescriptiveness of faculty professional development workshops: The Real-Time Professional Development Observation Tool (R-PDOT). arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.07126v2
title: Two-dimensional coding of workshop engagement: type of engagement crossed with focus of engagement
description: The R-PDOT captures workshop sessions along two complementary dimensions at once: how faculty are engaged (lecture, small group, large group discussion, presentations, independent work) and what their attention is focused on (e.g., education research theory, simulated instructional strategies, past experiences, student experiences, planning for future teaching). Unlike type-of-engagement codes, "more than one focus-of-engagement code can occur simultaneously for faculty—these categories are not exclusive." The pattern lets leaders examine the intersection of the two dimensions rather than each in isolation.
requirements: Codes broad enough that an observer can record them quickly with reasonable fidelity in real time
constraints: Individual codes are broad in scope, so a single code could be enacted in a variety of ways
target_learning_goals: Designing and evaluating workshop sessions that support both awareness-level and emergent (reflective) faculty outcomes
examples: Table III lists the eleven focus-of-engagement codes with brief descriptions, from Workshop Instructions through Planning for FP Future Teaching
key_sources: Alice Olmstead and Chandra Turpen. (2016). Assessing the interactivity and prescriptiveness of faculty professional development workshops: The Real-Time Professional Development Observation Tool (R-PDOT). arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.07126
